source: Dalal et al. (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (IBE-Eval)
finding: IBE-Eval scores competing LLM-written explanations on four code-computed features: logical consistency (Prolog solver), parsimony (proof depth, concept drift), coherence (mean step entailment), and linguistic uncertainty. It picks the more plausible explanation by a fitted combination.
numbers: Tasks COPA and E-CARE (500 sampled test items each); models GPT-3.5-turbo, LLaMA 2 13B, LLaMA 2 7B. Best accuracy 77% (GPT-3.5, COPA), 27 points above random; +17.5% on average over a GPT-3.5-as-judge baseline.
limits: Causal multiple-choice QA with two options only. The 'coherence' here is step-wise entailment, not Thagard's explanatory coherence. Features are fitted, so the 77% is on the authors' split.
agent_relevance: Direct template for 'selection by code': score hypotheses with computed consistency, simplicity, coherence and hedging, not with a model verdict.

source: Dalal et al. (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (IBE-Eval) (ablation)
finding: Each feature alone is weak. Adding features one by one raises accuracy. The composed model beats the judge baseline.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on COPA: consistency alone .51, depth .67, drift .67, coherence .66, uncertainty .70; composed .77. GPT-3.5-as-judge about .59 on COPA. LLaMA 2 13B and 7B composed scores .65 to .74 (table columns interleaved in extraction).
limits: Table read from pdftotext layout; some model-to-cell mappings are approximate.
agent_relevance: Features must be combined; no single acceptance criterion is enough. Matches coverage + coherence + uniqueness as a bundle.

source: Dalal et al. (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (IBE-Eval) (consistency)
finding: Logical consistency does not discriminate: models write logically consistent explanations for wrong answers as often as for right ones. Consistency is an insignificant predictor for the LLaMA models.
numbers: Consistency-only accuracy .51 to .55 on most cells.
limits: LLMs are strong rationalizers. A check that only tests internal consistency is not evidence.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: a story that hangs together proves nothing. Consistency must be tested against data the story was not built from.

source: Dalal et al. (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (IBE-Eval) (uncertainty)
finding: Hedging language is the strongest single predictor. Explanations for the weaker option contain more epistemic hedges. Parsimony (fewer steps, less concept drift) and coherence also favor the correct answer.
numbers: Uncertainty-only accuracy up to .70 (GPT-3.5, COPA). Negative correlation with accuracy, p<0.001 for GPT-3.5.
limits: Hedge counts are a surface cue and could be gamed by prompting.
agent_relevance: A cheap code feature: model hesitancy while building a story is informative about its fit. Use as a tie-breaker in S7.

source: Dalal et al. (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (IBE-Eval) (human check)
finding: IBE-Eval tracks human judgments of explanation plausibility far better than a GPT-3.5 judge.
numbers: 100 explanation pairs, 2 human raters: pick correct explanation 96% (COPA), 91% (E-CARE); kappa .68. Spearman with humans: IBE-Eval 0.64 (p<0.01) vs GPT-3.5 judge 0.31 (n.s.).
limits: Small sample; two raters; only two datasets.
agent_relevance: Evidence that code-computed acceptance features beat model self-judgment (G5).

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (BBS 12:435-502)
finding: ECHO is a localist connectionist network. Propositions are units; explanation and analogy give excitatory links; contradiction and competition give inhibitory links; evidence units get data excitation. After settling, positive activation means acceptance, negative means rejection. Uniqueness is built in as competition between hypotheses explaining the same evidence.
numbers: Default parameters: excitation .05, inhibition -.2, data excitation .1, decay .05, simplicity impact 1. Runs on Lavoisier, Chambers (preppy murder) and Peyer trials.
quote: positive activation can be interpreted as acceptance of the proposition
limits: Many free parameters; commentators (Earle) say this limits testability. Input propositions are hand-coded.
agent_relevance: The ECHO update rule is a few lines of code. It is a ready code-selects module for hypothesis acceptance (S7) once the model lists hypotheses, evidence and explain/contradict links.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (BBS 12:435-502) (Peyer trial)
finding: ECHO modelled the Peyer murder trial, which ended in a hung jury (7 for conviction, 5 against). ECHO found more coherence in the guilt hypotheses but rejected innocence much less strongly than in the Chambers case, matching reluctance to convict beyond doubt.
numbers: Hung jury 7-5. Sensitivity Table 11 shows weaker rejection of innocence than in Chambers.
limits: Case study from newspaper coverage with hand-coded input; post-hoc, not a prospective prediction.
agent_relevance: Shows a calibrated outcome: a weak margin between rival stories should give low confidence, not a forced pick.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (BBS 12:435-502) (sensitivity)
finding: Results in the Lavoisier example do not change when decay, excitation, inhibition and data excitation are all halved or doubled. Higher decay flattens activation; higher data excitation raises evidence activation.
numbers: Parameters halved or doubled: no important differences in the Lavoisier run.
limits: Only some examples tested; commentators doubt the model is fixed by data rather than flexible.
agent_relevance: Acceptance ranking should be checked for stability under parameter changes before being trusted (cheap robustness test by code).

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (BBS 12:435-502) (commentaries: order effects, free parameters)
finding: A peer commentary notes that Pennington and Hastie found evidence order changes verdicts, which a Bayesian analysis forbids. Another commentary says ECHO has many free parameters, making it flexible and hard to test.
numbers: No numbers; qualitative critique.
limits: Commentary, not experiment.
agent_relevance: Order effects are a known deviation of coherence-based acceptance from Bayes: shuffle evidence order as a stability check.

source: Thagard (1989) ECHO principles as a reading of Pennington and Hastie
finding: Thagard uses Pennington and Hastie's finding (jury belief depends on explanatory coherence of the prosecution story) as a motivating case for seven principles: symmetry, explanation, analogy, data priority, contradiction, competition, acceptability.
numbers: Seven principles; text opened.
limits: Thagard's reading of the story model, not a replication of it.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact criteria list (coherence, competition = uniqueness) that can be coded.

source: Huntsman and Thomas (2025) Benchmarking graph construction by LLMs for coherence-driven inference
finding: Coherence maximisation is MAX-CUT on the negated weighted adjacency matrix: split propositions into accepted and rejected sets to cut the most negative edges. The authors generate propositions that objectively instantiate a known coherence graph and test whether LLMs rebuild it.
numbers: 76 graphs (38 sparse, 38 dense), 5 to 23 nodes; sparse median edge density 0.202, dense 0.734. o1-mini, o3-mini, o4-mini reach perfect reconstruction about half the time on sparse graphs; claude-3.5-sonnet and QwQ-32B also have high micro F1. Hallucinated extra propositions: gemini-2.0-flash-exp 10 of 608 attempts, gpt-4o 5, gemini-1.5-pro 4.
limits: Synthetic propositions with +1/-1 edges; not real legal text. Authors say real-world results are too preliminary to report.
agent_relevance: Split of labour fits the schema: model judges pair consistency locally, code solves the global accept/reject.

source: Huntsman and Thomas (2025) Benchmarking graph construction by LLMs for coherence-driven inference (density effect)
finding: Reconstruction fidelity depends strongly on graph density and on model. Two-way ANOVA on micro F1 shows significant effects of model and density.
numbers: Density F=369.50 (p<0.001); model x density interaction p<0.001.
limits: Statistics partly read from appendix.
agent_relevance: Dense conflict graphs are where LLM pairwise judging fails; keep the hypothesis set small.

source: Huntsman (2025) Automatic coherence-driven inference on arguments
finding: Pipeline: an LLM extracts propositions from an argument and rates pairwise consistency; combinatorial optimisation then finds the max-coherence accepted/rejected partition. Applied to the Melian Dialogue, a 2025 Oval Office meeting and Brown v. Board oral argument.
numbers: Case demonstrations with GPT-4o and o1-mini, median graph over repeated runs; ChatGPT 4 consistency ratings improved on an earlier expert baseline. No accuracy table.
limits: Illustrative, no ground-truth benchmark.
agent_relevance: A tested pattern for an LLM agent loop: LLM labels pair relations, code does the global selection.

source: Huntsman (2025) Automatic coherence-driven inference on arguments (reproducibility)
finding: Because LLM edge weights vary run to run, the author takes median weights over repeated runs to get a stable result. Near-optimal alternative partitions can exist (Rashomon), handled by averaging over a Gibbs measure.
numbers: Repeated runs used; exact count not extracted.
limits: Method note.
agent_relevance: Repeat the pairwise judgments and take a median; report acceptance as a probability, not a hard flag.

source: Jung et al. (2022) Maieutic Prompting
finding: GPT-3 generates abductive explanation trees (X is true because ...), a verifier scores belief and consistency, and a weighted MAX-SAT solver finds the most coherent truth assignment. This is explanatory-coherence selection by code.
numbers: Com2Sense dev: Maieutic 72.5 vs CoT 61.6, Self-Consistency 61.4, GKP 61.8, standard 58.1. CSQA 2.0: 69.5 vs 59.6 and 60.8. CREAK: 85.2 vs 64.8 and 70.5. Up to 20% over prompting baselines. Ablation (Com2Sense): non-abductive generation 68.4; likelihood-based consistency 65.6. Verifier RoBERTa-large MNLI 90.2%; solver RC2.
limits: text-davinci-001 only; true/false QA only; table columns partly garbled in extraction. Weights fixed to 1 worked better.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct LLM test of coherence as constraint satisfaction. A MAX-SAT acceptance step beats majority vote on commonsense QA.

source: Kassner et al. (2021) BeliefBank
finding: A weighted MaxSAT solver over a store of model answers and logical constraints revises clashing beliefs; feeding relevant stored beliefs back as context helps further.
numbers: Constraint solving: consistency about 95%, +17% accuracy (F1) over raw model. Feedback plus constraints: +18% F1. Random off-topic feedback: no gain (72% F1, 74% consistency after batch 10).
limits: T5-large era model; synthetic taxonomic constraints; false positives high (precision 54%, recall 98% in failure analysis).
agent_relevance: Coherence repair by code works, but needs correct constraints and is bounded by the model's wrong beliefs.

source: Tafjord et al. (2022) Entailer
finding: Entailer builds backward-chaining proof trees and only accepts premises the model itself believes (self-queried), scoring the best-supported hypothesis.
numbers: Users judge 70%+ of chains clearly show how the answer follows; zero-shot OBQA about 75% vs GPT-3 reported 57.6% zero-shot and 65.4% few-shot. Fallback to direct answer on 16.8% (OBQA) and 14.2% (QuaRTz) of questions. Reasoning errors 47% of failures.
limits: Small QA datasets; the belief verifier is the same model family, so errors are shared.
agent_relevance: Support for requiring each premise of a story to pass a belief check before acceptance.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking a majority vote over final answers is a crude agreement (uniqueness-like) acceptance rule. It improves chain of thought.
numbers: Absolute gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9. Normalised weighted sum beats unnormalised.
limits: Samples from one model are correlated (our G4); agreement is a hint, not proof.
agent_relevance: Agreement across samples is the cheap form of uniqueness. Use as signal only.

source: Wu (2026) When Does Defendant Statement Matter? JuryBench
finding: 20 frontier LLMs simulate jurors on controversial cases. Emotional persuasion can backfire as perceived inconsistency; juror-defendant background match and juror ideology strongly shift severity.
numbers: 432K decisions and rationales; 20 models; juror ideology from -5 to +5; model severity-bias scores range from +0.55 (Gemini 3 Flash) to -0.59 (Qwen3).
limits: Persona prompts; no real juror data; not a story-model test.
agent_relevance: LLM jurors are moved by persona and emotional cues, not only by story fit. Do not use persona voters (G4).

source: Anon. (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents
finding: Multi-agent LLM jury deliberation rarely reaches a verdict. Agents recite evidence and do not integrate counter-arguments (parallel monologues), so consensus acceptance fails.
numbers: 17 of 18 runs hung (94%). GPT-4o: 9 of 9 hung, mean vote changes 1.0, 0.7, 1.0 across three conditions. Llama-4-Scout: 8 hung, 1 acquittal in 64 turns; vote changes 2.0 (baseline), 3.3 (no initial vote), 6.0 (open-minded prompt). N=3 per cell.
limits: Exploratory, tiny N per cell, two models, one film scenario (paper's own limitations).
agent_relevance: Debate between instances is a weak acceptance mechanism; code-side scoring is better than agents arguing to consensus.

source: LLM story-model coding study (Univ. Turku repository; ChatGPT vs Gemini on one deliberation transcript)
finding: Per a search summary only: LLMs coded one transcript against Story Model functions; ChatGPT precision 72.7%; Gemini had many false positives on causal links.
numbers: Precision 72.7% (ChatGPT), from snippet only; page blocked by bot check.
limits: Single transcript; unverified.
agent_relevance: Possible check on whether LLMs can code story structure; do not rely on it.

source: Mock jury replication with GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1 (Law and Human Behavior, 2025)
finding: Per a search summary only: a 2025 paper replicated a mock jury experiment with these LLMs as decision-makers.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Not opened; title and results unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: Candidate to find later for direct human-versus-LLM juror comparison.

source: Search gap: no direct test of story coverage, coherence and uniqueness in LLMs
finding: Searches (shared budget ran out; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv API were rate-limited) found no study testing whether LLM verdicts follow story coverage, coherence and uniqueness as Pennington and Hastie define them.
numbers: None.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search.
agent_relevance: Open gap: build a small test where two stories fit equally well and see whether model confidence drops (uniqueness).

source: Jung et al. (2022) Maieutic Prompting (error analysis)
finding: GPT-3 explanations are often logically inconsistent: about 41% of sampled wrong cases involve explanations that do not support the model's own answer, and models can justify both a statement and its negation. This is why a consistency solver over many explanations helps.
numbers: Figure 1 error types: Type I 41%, Type II 33%, Type III 35% of 100 manually checked questions.
limits: Manual check of 100 questions; categories may overlap.
agent_relevance: One explanation is not an acceptance basis; check pairs of statements for conflict by code.

source: Dalal et al. (2024) IBE-Eval (limits)
finding: Self-evident or tautologous explanations could game parsimony, but they caused under 0.1% of errors. Effects are strongest for GPT-3.5 and weaker for smaller LLaMA models.
numbers: Self-evident explanations: 2% generated; under 0.1% of selection errors.
limits: Two-option tasks; no uniqueness test with three or more near-equal rivals.
agent_relevance: Note: parsimony and coherence scores are robust to cheap gaming here, but uniqueness (margin between top rivals) was not tested.
